subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Network Virtualization, Availability, Performance and Security

subjective.question: Define IT infrastructure.
subjective.answer: IT infrastructure consists of the equipment, systems, software, and services used in common across an organization, regardless of mission, program or project. It also serves as the foundation upon which mission/program/project-specific systems and capabilities are built. There is no single generally accepted definition of IT infrastructure; what it comprises depends on who you ask and what their point of view is.

subjective.question: List the various kinds of architecture discussed in the course.
subjective.answer: The kinds of architecture are: (1) Business architecture, (2) Enterprise architecture, (3) Data architecture, (4) Application architecture, and (5) Infrastructure architecture.

subjective.question: What are non-functional attributes? List the non-functional attributes of IT infrastructure.
subjective.answer: Non-functional attributes describe the qualitative behavior of a system rather than its specific functionality. They include: Availability, Security, Performance, Recoverability, Testability and Scalability. Although infrastructure services such as disk space, processing and connectivity can be defined as functions, most of these services are non-functional in nature.

subjective.question: How should conflicting non-functional requirements (NFRs) be handled?
subjective.answer: It is not unusual to encounter conflicting NFRs; for instance, users may want a system that is secure but not want to be bothered by passwords. It is the task of the infrastructure architect to balance these NFRs. In some cases some NFRs may take priority over others, and the architect must involve the relevant stakeholders in these decisions.

subjective.question: Define availability. Why can 100% availability never be guaranteed?
subjective.answer: Availability is usually expressed as a percentage of uptime in a given time period, usually one year or one month. For example, 99.9% (three nines) allows 8.8 hours of downtime per year, 99.99% (four nines) allows 52.6 minutes per year, and 99.999% (five nines, also called carrier grade availability) allows only 5.3 minutes per year. Availability can neither be calculated nor guaranteed upfront; it can only be reported on afterwards, when a system has run for some years.

subjective.question: Define MTBF and MTTR. Write the formula for calculating availability with an example.
subjective.answer: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) is the average time that passes between failures. MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) is the time it takes to recover from a failure. Availability is calculated as: Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR) x 100%. Example: a power supply with MTBF 100,000 hours and MTTR 8 hours has an availability of 100,000 / 100,008 x 100% = 99.992%.

subjective.question: How can MTTR be kept low? List the steps needed to complete a repair.
subjective.answer: MTTR can be kept low by: (1) having a service contract with the supplier, (2) having spare parts on-site, and (3) automated redundancy and failover. The repair itself consists of steps: notification of the fault, processing the alarm, finding the root cause of the error, looking up repair information, getting spare components from storage, having a technician come to the datacenter with the spare component, physically repairing the fault, and restarting and testing the component.

subjective.question: Differentiate between serial and parallel availability calculations.
subjective.answer: For serial components, one defect leads to downtime, so the total availability is the product of the individual availabilities (e.g. 0.99992 x 0.99992 x ... = 99.977% for a chain of components). For parallel components, one defect causes no downtime; the combined availability is A = 1 - (1 - A1)^n. For example, two parallel components of 99% each give 1 - (1 - 0.99)^2 = 99.99%. However, in parallel setups one must beware of SPOFs.

subjective.question: Discuss the major sources of unavailability in an IT infrastructure.
subjective.answer: The main sources of unavailability are: (1) Human errors - about 80% of outages impacting mission-critical services are caused by people and process issues, e.g. switching off the wrong component or restoring the wrong backup tape. (2) Software bugs - because of the complexity of software it is nearly impossible to create bug-free software. (3) Planned maintenance - during maintenance the system is more vulnerable and a temporary SPOF could be introduced. (4) Physical defects - everything breaks down eventually; mechanical parts such as fans and disk drives break first. (5) Environmental issues - power, cooling, fire, earthquakes and flooding. (6) Complexity of the infrastructure - complex systems have more potential points of failure and are harder to manage.

subjective.question: Explain the bathtub curve and the term DOA.
subjective.answer: The bathtub curve describes how the failure rate of a component changes over its lifetime. A component failure is most likely when the component is new; sometimes a component does not work at all when unpacked for the first time, which is called a DOA component (Dead On Arrival). When a component still works after the first month, it is likely that it will continue working without failure until the end of its life, when the failure rate rises again.

subjective.question: What is a Single Point of Failure (SPOF)? How can SPOFs be eliminated?
subjective.answer: A Single Point of Failure (SPOF) is a component in the infrastructure that, if it fails, causes downtime to the entire system. SPOFs should be avoided because they pose a large risk to the availability of a system. To eliminate SPOFs, a combination of redundancy, failover and fallback is used: redundancy duplicates critical components within a single system (e.g. two power supplies, dual network interfaces), failover is the (semi)automatic switch-over to a standby system or component, and fallback is the manual switch-over to an identical standby system in a different location.

subjective.question: Differentiate between failover and fallback. Name the three basic forms of fallback solutions.
subjective.answer: Failover is the (semi)automatic switch-over to a standby system or component, for example Windows Server failover clustering or VMware High Availability. Fallback is the manual switch-over to an identical standby computer system in a different location and is typically used for disaster recovery. Fallback solutions have three basic forms: a hot site (fully equipped and ready to take over immediately), a warm site (partially equipped), and a cold site (space available but equipment must be installed first).

subjective.question: What is business continuity? Name the processes used to handle disasters.
subjective.answer: Business continuity is about identifying the threats an organization faces and providing an effective response, so that the business can continue when a disaster makes the infrastructure unavailable for a longer period. The two processes used are Business Continuity Management (BCM) and Disaster Recovery Planning (DRP). An IT disaster is defined as an irreparable problem in a datacenter, making the datacenter unusable, caused by natural disasters (floods, hurricanes, tornadoes, earthquakes) or manmade disasters (hazardous material spills, infrastructure failure, bio-terrorism).

subjective.question: What is perceived performance? How can it be improved for users?
subjective.answer: Perceived performance refers to how quickly a system appears to perform its task. In general, people tend to overestimate their own patience, and people tend to value predictability in performance: when the performance of a system fluctuates, users remember a bad experience even if the fluctuation is relatively rare. Users should be informed about how long a task will take, for example through progress bars and splash screens.

subjective.question: Describe the methods used to estimate performance during the infrastructure design phase.
subjective.answer: The main methods are: (1) Benchmarking - using a specific test program to assess the relative performance of an infrastructure component, e.g. FLOPS and MIPS for raw processor speed. (2) Prototyping (proof of concept) - measuring the performance of a system at an early stage, focusing on the parts that pose the highest risk. (3) Vendor experience - vendors have much experience running their products in various configurations and can provide tools, figures and best practices. (4) User profiling - predicting the load a new system will pose on the infrastructure by defining typical user groups (personas), listing their tasks, decomposing tasks into infrastructure actions, estimating the load per action and calculating the total load.

subjective.question: Explain the types of performance testing.
subjective.answer: Load testing shows how a system performs under the expected load. Stress testing shows how a system reacts when it is under extreme load. Endurance testing shows how a system behaves when it is used at the expected load for a long period of time. In a breakpoint test, the load is ramped up: the test starts with a small number of virtual users and increases the number over a period of time, showing how performance (response time) varies with the load. Performance testing should be done in a production-like environment, because results from a development environment are usually highly unreliable.

subjective.question: What is a bottleneck? What is the role of capacity management?
subjective.answer: A bottleneck is a component that causes the system to reach some limit; every system has at least one bottleneck that limits its performance. If the bottleneck does not negatively influence the performance of the complete system under the highest expected load, it is acceptable. Capacity management guarantees high performance of a system in the long term: performance must be monitored, trend analyses can be used to predict performance degradation, and business changes (like forthcoming marketing campaigns) should be anticipated.

subjective.question: How does caching improve performance? Explain the role of a web proxy.
subjective.answer: Caching stores data in fast memory so it can be fetched quickly. It can be implemented in disks, disk controllers and the operating system; cache memory stores all data recently read from disk and some of the disk blocks following it. The difference is large: fetching 1 MB takes about 105 ms from a hard disk, but only 0.2 ms from main memory (DDR3 RAM) and 0.016 ms from the CPU L1 cache. A web proxy server is a type of cache: earlier accessed data can be fetched from the cache instead of from the internet, so users get their data faster and more bandwidth to the internet remains available for other users.

subjective.question: What is grid computing? Give examples.
subjective.answer: A computer grid is a high performance cluster that consists of systems that are spread geographically. The limited bandwidth between the systems is the bottleneck. Examples are SETI@HOME and the CERN LHC Computing Grid (140 computing centers in 35 countries). Broker firms exist for the commercial exploitation of grids, and security is a concern when computers in the grid are not under the organization's control.

subjective.question: Explain the CIA triad of security goals.
subjective.answer: The CIA triad contains the three core goals of security. Confidentiality prevents the intentional or unintentional unauthorized disclosure of data. Integrity ensures that no modifications to data are made by unauthorized staff or processes, that unauthorized modifications are not made by authorized staff or processes either, and that data is consistent. Availability ensures the reliable and timely access to data or IT resources. Information can be classified on CIA levels (for example 1 to 5), and security controls must address at least one of the CIA goals.

subjective.question: Describe the risk management process and the elements of a risk list.
subjective.answer: Managing security is all about managing risks; the effort put into securing the infrastructure should be directly related to the risk at hand. Risk management is the process of: (1) determining an acceptable level of risk, (2) assessing the current level of risk, (3) taking steps to reduce risk to the acceptable level, and (4) maintaining that level. A risk list is used to quantify risks and contains the asset name, the vulnerability, the exploit, the probability of the exploit occurring, and the impact (severity of the damage).

subjective.question: What are the four risk responses?
subjective.answer: The four risk responses are: (1) Acceptance of the risk. (2) Avoidance of the risk - do not perform actions that impose risk. (3) Transfer of the risk - for instance, transfer the risk to an insurance company. (4) Mitigation of the risk and accepting the residual risk. Controls can be designed and implemented based on the identified severity of the risk in the risk list.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a virus, a worm and a Trojan Horse. What is a DDoS attack?
subjective.answer: A virus is a self-replicating program fragment that attaches itself to a program or file, enabling it to spread from one computer to another. A worm is a self-replicating program that spreads from one computer to another on its own, leaving infections as it travels. A Trojan Horse appears to be useful software but will actually do damage once installed or run on the computer. A Denial of Service (DoS) attack attempts to overload an infrastructure to cause disruption of a service; in a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack, the attacker uses many computers, and groups of infected computers called botnets perform the attack.

subjective.question: Explain the three steps of the Identity and Access Management (IAM) process.
subjective.answer: Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the process of managing the identity of people and systems, and their permissions. The IAM process follows three steps: (1) Identification - users or systems claim who they are. (2) Authentication - the claimed identity is checked. (3) Authorization - permissions are granted related to the identity and the groups it belongs to.

subjective.question: What is layered security (Defense-in-Depth)? State its disadvantage.
subjective.answer: Layered security, also known as a Defense-In-Depth strategy, implements various security measures in various parts of the IT infrastructure. Instead of having one big firewall and having all security depend on it, several layers of security are implemented, preferably using different technologies. This makes it harder for hackers to break through all barriers, as they will need specific knowledge for each step. Its disadvantage is that it increases the complexity of the system.

subjective.question: Define cryptography, encryption and a cipher. Differentiate between block ciphers and stream ciphers.
subjective.answer: Cryptography is the practice of hiding information using encryption and decryption techniques. Encryption is the conversion of information from a readable state to apparent random data; only the receiver can decrypt it back to the original information. A cipher is a pair of algorithms that implements the encryption and decryption process, and its operation is controlled by a key. Block ciphers encrypt a block of plaintext with a key into a block of cipher text (standards: DES and AES) and are used from ATM machine data encryption to e-mail privacy. Stream ciphers create an arbitrarily long stream of key material and combine it with the plaintext bit-by-bit or character-by-character; they are used when data is in transit over the network, and RC4 is a widely-used stream cipher.

subjective.question: List and describe the categories of datacenters.
subjective.answer: The typical datacenter categories are: (1) Sub Equipment Room (SER), also known as a patch closet. (2) Main Equipment Room (MER), a small datacenter in the organization's subsidiaries or buildings. (3) Organization owned datacenter, which contains all central IT equipment for the organization. (4) Multi-tenant datacenter, used by service providers that provide services for multiple other organizations; these datacenters are typically the largest.

subjective.question: Explain the backup power systems used in a datacenter (UPS and generators).
subjective.answer: Backup power in a datacenter consists of an Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) and power generators. A UPS is independent of the utility power supply and provides power for a short period of time, bridging the gap until generators start. Power generators can power the datacenter for an indefinite period of time, as long as fuel is available. Types of power issues in the utility supply include blackouts, surges, spikes and waveform issues, which can lead to downtime and damage to equipment. Power is distributed by Power Distribution Units (PDUs): large floor-mounted PDUs that take main feeds and distribute them into smaller feeds to racks, and power strips that feed equipment in racks.

subjective.question: What is PUE? How is it calculated and what are its typical values?
subjective.answer: Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) is the metric that measures the power used by the datacenter. It is calculated by dividing the total amount of power used by the datacenter by the power used to run the IT equipment in it. A typical PUE value of a datacenter is between 1.1 and 2.0; the closer the value is to 1.0, the more efficient the datacenter is, because less power is spent on cooling and other overhead. Note that about 90% of all power used by IT infrastructure components is converted into heat, which has to be dissipated by the cooling system (CRAC refrigerant-based units or CRAH units using chilled water).

subjective.question: Compare the four datacenter availability tiers.
subjective.answer: Datacenters are classified into four availability tiers. Tier 1 (Basic, 99.671%): a single path for power and cooling distribution, no redundant components; downtime is very likely for planned and unplanned maintenance. Tier 2 (Redundant components, 99.741%): fulfills all Tier 1 requirements and adds redundant components, but still a single distribution path. Tier 3 (Concurrently maintainable, 99.982%): multiple active power and cooling distribution paths with only one path active and redundant components; no downtime due to planned maintenance, and all IT equipment must be dual-powered. Tier 4 (Fault tolerant, 99.995%): fulfills all previous tiers, with multiple active paths, redundant components and all cooling equipment independently dual-powered; no downtime due to planned or unplanned maintenance.

subjective.question: What is the OSI Reference Model? Name its seven layers with one function or example for each.
subjective.answer: The OSI Reference Model was developed in 1984 by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). Its seven layers define the different stages that data must go through to travel from one host to another over a network: (1) Physical layer - cables and signals. (2) Data link layer - e.g. Ethernet, switching by MAC address. (3) Network layer - e.g. the IP protocol and routing. (4) Transport layer - e.g. TCP and UDP, flow control and error checking. (5) Session layer - opening, closing and managing sessions between application processes. (6) Presentation layer - converting data into a standard format, e.g. SSL/TLS. (7) Application layer - protocols such as HTTP, FTP and SMTP, plus infrastructure services like DHCP, DNS and NTP. The OSI stack allows network components to be implemented independently of each other while ensuring that all components work together.

subjective.question: Explain how CSMA/CD works.
subjective.answer: CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) is the access method used on a shared carrier such as a coax cable, a twisted-pair hub or the Wi-Fi radio spectrum. Any machine can start transmitting packets when the shared carrier is not in use; carrier sensing circuitry checks the activity on the carrier. When two machines start to transmit a packet at the same time, a packet collision occurs. This is detected by all sending machines; they will stop the transmission immediately, and after a short waiting time they will retransmit their packet when the carrier is not in use anymore.

subjective.question: Explain IPv4 addressing, its classes, subnetting and the private IP ranges.
subjective.answer: An IPv4 address is composed of 4 bytes (32 bits) and consists of a network prefix and a host number. Three classes are defined: Class A (first byte 0-127, 128 networks, 16,777,214 hosts), Class B (first byte 128-191, 16,384 networks, 65,534 hosts) and Class C (first byte 192-223, 2,097,152 networks, 254 hosts). Subnetting (using CIDR prefixes) splits up the host part of an IP network into smaller subnets, each forming a new IP network; for example a /26 subnet with mask 255.255.255.192 provides 62 usable hosts per subnet. Private IP ranges, which are not used on the internet and are not routed by internet routers, are: 10.0.0.0-10.255.255.255 (Class A), 172.16.0.0-172.31.255.255 (Class B) and 192.168.0.0-192.168.255.255 (Class C).

subjective.question: Why was IPv6 introduced? Write its features and deployment models.
subjective.answer: IPv6 was introduced in 1998 as the successor of IPv4 to solve the problem of limited IP address space. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, represented in eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons, for example 2001:0bb8:86a2:0000:0000:8b1e:1350:7c34. Its benefits include expanded address space, better support for mobile IP, fixed header length, auto configuration, Quality of Service, security and MTU discovery. IPv6 is not backwards compatible with IPv4; deployment models include using IPv6 on the LAN and on dedicated WAN links, protocol translation, dual stack (the simplest way to begin deploying IPv6) and IPv6 over IPv4 tunnels.

subjective.question: Compare TCP and UDP.
subjective.answer: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) uses the IP protocol to create reliable transmission: it provides reliable, ordered delivery of a stream of data between applications, but introduces much overhead. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) emphasizes reduced latency over reliability; it sends data without checking if the data arrived, which reduces overhead. UDP is typically used when some packet loss is acceptable, for example real-time voice and video streams, and when only small amounts of data are transmitted that fit in one IP packet. Both TCP and UDP use logical port numbers between 0 and 65,535; well-known ports include FTP (21), SSH (22), SMTP (25), DNS (53) and HTTP (80).

subjective.question: Differentiate between BOOTP and DHCP.
subjective.answer: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is an extension of BOOTP. BOOTP automatically assigns IP addresses to hosts using a centralized BOOTP server, but it requires manual configuration for each host in the network. DHCP superseded BOOTP because it has more options: it dynamically assigns network related parameters to hosts, including IP addresses, subnet masks, the default gateway to be used for routing, and the DNS server to be used. A DHCP-assigned IP address has a limited life span, typically a few hours, which is called a lease.

subjective.question: Explain the roles of DNS and NTP in an IT infrastructure.
subjective.answer: DNS (Domain Name System) is a distributed database that links IP addresses with domain names; it translates domain names, which are meaningful to humans, into IP addresses used by browsers to connect to web servers, and it distributes this responsibility by designating authoritative name servers for each domain. NTP (Network Time Protocol) ensures all infrastructure components use the same time in their real-time clocks, which is particularly important for log file analysis, clustering software and Kerberos authentication. NTP can maintain time to within 10 milliseconds over the internet and to 0.2 milliseconds or better in LANs; it provides time in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), and each level in its hierarchy is assigned a stratum number that defines its distance from the reference clock.

subjective.topic: Network Virtualization, Availability, Performance and Security
subjective.question: What is network virtualization?
subjective.answer: Network virtualization abstracts network resources that were traditionally delivered in hardware to software. It decouples network services from the underlying hardware and allows virtual provisioning of an entire network: multiple physical networks can be combined into one virtual, software-based network, or one physical network can be divided into separate, independent virtual networks. Physical network resources such as switching, routing, firewalling, load balancing and VPNs are pooled and delivered in software, requiring only IP packet forwarding from the underlying physical network.

subjective.topic: Network Virtualization, Availability, Performance and Security
subjective.question: What is a VLAN? How does VXLAN differ from a VLAN?
subjective.answer: VLANs (Virtual LANs) enable logical grouping of network nodes on the same LAN. They are configured on network switches and operate at the Ethernet (data link) level. VLANs allow segmenting a network at the data link layer, allow end stations to be grouped together even if they are not physically connected to the same switch, can adapt to changes in network requirements with simplified administration, and enhance security by preventing traffic in one VLAN from being seen by hosts in a different VLAN. For VLANs to communicate with each other, a router is needed. VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN) is an encapsulation protocol that can be used to create a logical switched layer 2 network across routed layer 3 networks; it is heavily used in multi-tenant cloud environments.

subjective.topic: Network Virtualization, Availability, Performance and Security
subjective.question: Explain Software Defined Networking (SDN). Differentiate between the control plane and the data plane.
subjective.answer: Software Defined Networking (SDN) allows networks to be defined and controlled using software external to the physical networking devices. In SDN, the software is decoupled from the hardware: SDN moves the control plane, which determines where to send traffic, to software (centralized in the SDN controller), and leaves the data plane, which actually forwards the traffic, in the hardware (distributed physical switches). This allows network administrators to program and control the entire network via a single pane of glass (a single management console) instead of on a device-by-device basis, and the physical devices become much simpler and more cost effective because they only forward packets based on rules preloaded by the SDN controller.

subjective.topic: Network Virtualization, Availability, Performance and Security
subjective.question: Describe the layered network topology (core, distribution and access layers).
subjective.answer: A network infrastructure should be built up in layers to improve availability and performance, provide scalability and deterministic routing, and avoid unmanaged ad-hoc data streams. The three layers are: (1) Core layer - the center of the network. (2) Distribution layer - an intermediate layer between the core layer in the datacenter and the access switches in the patch closets; it combines the access layer data and sends it to one or two ports on the core switches. (3) Access layer - connects workstations and servers to the distribution layer; for servers it is located at the top of the individual server racks or in blade enclosures, and for workstations in patch closets. Because the layering provides multiple paths to any piece of equipment, it provides high availability.

subjective.topic: Network Virtualization, Availability, Performance and Security
subjective.question: Write the characteristics and benefits of the spine and leaf topology.
subjective.answer: The characteristics of the spine and leaf topology are: the spine switches are not interconnected; each leaf switch is connected to all spine switches; each server is connected to two leaf switches; and the connections between spine and leaf switches typically have ten times the bandwidth of the connectivity between the leaf switches and the servers. Its benefits are: it is highly scalable because there are no interconnects between the spine switches; it is simple to scale by just adding spine or leaf switches; many physical servers can be connected using relatively few switches; and each server is always exactly four hops away from every other server, which leads to a very predictable latency.

subjective.topic: Network Virtualization, Availability, Performance and Security
subjective.question: What is the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)? State its disadvantage and how RSTP improves it.
subjective.answer: The Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) is an Ethernet level protocol that runs on switches. It guarantees that only one path is active between two network endpoints at any given time, and redundant paths are automatically activated when the active path experiences problems. This ensures that no loops are created when redundant paths are available in the network. A disadvantage of STP is that it does not use half of the network links, since it blocks redundant paths. Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (RSTP) provides faster spanning tree convergence after a topology change (about 6 seconds instead of 30 seconds).

subjective.topic: Network Virtualization, Availability, Performance and Security
subjective.question: What is Quality of Service (QoS)? Describe the four basic ways to implement QoS.
subjective.answer: Quality of Service (QoS) is the ability to provide different data flow priority to different applications, users, or types of data; it allows better service to certain important data flows compared to less important data flows, and it is mainly used for real-time applications like video and audio streams and VoIP telephony. The four basic ways to implement QoS are: (1) Congestion management - defines what must be done if the amount of data to be sent exceeds the bandwidth of the network link; packets can either be dropped or queued. (2) Queue management - defines criteria for dropping packets of lower priority before dropping higher priority packets when queues are full. (3) Link efficiency - ensures the link is used in an optimized way, for instance by fragmenting large low-QoS packets so high-QoS packets can be sent between the fragments. (4) Traffic shaping - limiting the full bandwidth of streams with a low QoS to benefit streams with a high QoS, which have a reserved amount of bandwidth.

subjective.topic: Network Virtualization, Availability, Performance and Security
subjective.question: What is a firewall? Describe the methods firewalls use to control traffic.
subjective.answer: Firewalls separate two or more LAN or WAN segments for security reasons; they block all unpermitted network traffic between network segments, and permitted traffic must be explicitly enabled. Firewalls use three methods to control traffic: (1) Packet filtering - data packets are analyzed using preconfigured filters. (2) Proxy (application layer firewalls) - a proxy terminates the session on the application level on behalf of the server or the client and creates a new session. (3) Stateful inspection - inspects the placement of each individual packet within a packet stream and maintains records of all connections passing through the firewall. Firewalls can be implemented in hardware appliances, as an application on physical servers, or in virtual machines; host-based firewalls protect a server or end user computer and are part of the operating system.

subjective.topic: Network Virtualization, Availability, Performance and Security
subjective.question: Differentiate between NIDS and HIDS.
subjective.answer: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) or Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) detects and, if possible, prevents activities that compromise system security or are a hacking attempt; it monitors for suspicious activity and alerts the systems manager. An IPS can also stop attacks by changing firewall rules on the fly. There are two types: a Network-based IDS (NIDS) is placed at a strategic point in the network and monitors traffic to and from all devices on that network; it is not part of the network flow but just looks at it, to avoid detection by hackers. A Host-based IDS (HIDS) runs on individual servers or network devices; it monitors the network traffic of that device and also monitors user behavior and the alteration of critical (system) files.

subjective.topic: Network Virtualization, Availability, Performance and Security
subjective.question: What is a DMZ?
subjective.answer: A DMZ (De-Militarized Zone), also known as a screened subnet or the Perimeter Network, is a network that serves as a buffer between a secure protected internal network and the insecure internet. Public-facing services are placed in the DMZ so that even if they are compromised, the internal network remains protected behind another firewall layer.
